title: HackerRank in a String
directAnswer: Check whether the fixed word "hackerrank" appears as a subsequence (not substring) of the input. Walk one pointer through the input and a second pointer through "hackerrank"; whenever the current input character matches the current target character, advance the target pointer. If the target pointer reaches the end, every letter was matched in order → "YES", otherwise "NO". O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Greedy subsequence matching with two pointers
remember.formula:
j = 0; pat = "hackerrank"
for c in s:
    if j < len(pat) and c == pat[j]: j++
return "YES" if j == len(pat) else "NO"
rules: It's a **subsequence** check — characters must appear in order but **not** contiguously.
Advance the pattern pointer **only** on a match; never skip a needed letter.
Greedy (take the earliest match) is provably optimal for subsequence existence.
Success condition is `j == len(pattern)` after the scan, not reaching the end of `s`.
Note `hackerrank` has a double `r` — both must be matched in sequence.
whenToUse: Test whether a fixed pattern is a subsequence of a larger string
Order matters but gaps are allowed between matched characters
Single pass, O(1) extra space is desired
Matching is greedy — earliest valid character is always safe to take
antiSignals: Pattern must be contiguous → substring search (KMP / indexOf), not subsequence
Count the number of distinct subsequence matches → DP, not a single greedy pass
Find the shortest window containing the pattern → sliding window
Pattern is not fixed and very long → still O(n·m) greedy, fine, but think about it
remember.takeaway: Subsequence existence is a one-pass greedy: keep a pointer into the pattern and bump it on each match. Taking the earliest possible match never hurts — it leaves the most of the input for the remaining pattern letters. Reaching the pattern's end means success.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize subsequence (order-preserving, gaps allowed) versus substring (contiguous), and implement the greedy two-pointer match correctly including the double 'r'.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Treating it as a substring/contains check, or advancing the pattern pointer even when characters don't match, or testing the wrong success condition (end of s instead of end of pattern).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Say why greedy is correct: taking the earliest match for each pattern letter is never worse than waiting, because it preserves the maximum remaining suffix of s for the rest of the pattern.

problemStatement:
Given a string `s`, determine whether it contains the word `"hackerrank"` as a **subsequence** — that is, whether you can obtain `"hackerrank"` by deleting zero or more characters from `s` without reordering the rest.

Return `"YES"` if it does, `"NO"` otherwise.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
The target word is the fixed string "hackerrank" (length 10)
understanding: Subsequence means the letters of "hackerrank" must appear in s in the same relative order, but not necessarily next to each other. So we hunt for an 'h', then somewhere after it an 'a', then a 'c', and so on through the whole word. If we can thread all ten letters in order, the answer is YES.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Subsequence or substring?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Subsequence — characters in order with arbitrary gaps allowed. 'hhaacckk…' qualifies even though 'hackerrank' isn't contiguous.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the target always exactly 'hackerrank'?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — a fixed 10-letter word with a double 'r'. Both 'r's must be matched.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Case sensitivity?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: All lowercase, so no normalization needed.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if s is shorter than 10 characters?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Then it can't contain all ten letters in order → NO. The pointer simply never reaches the end of the pattern.

examples.explanation: Thread h-a-c-k-e-r-r-a-n-k through: h(0)…a…c…k…e…r…r…a…n…k all appear in order, so 'hackerrank' is a subsequence.
We match h,a,c,k,e,r but then need a second 'r' followed by a-n-k; 'world' provides none of that in order → NO.
Greedy matches h(0), a(2), c(4), k(6), e(8), r(10), r(12), a(13), n(15), k(17) — all ten letters in order.

approaches.name: Recursive Subsequence Check (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention to show you understand the recursive subsequence definition, then note the greedy one-pass is simpler and avoids overhead.
hints: Define match(i, j): can pat[j:] be a subsequence of s[i:]?
If pat[j] == s[i], you may consume both; you may also always skip s[i]. Recurse.
Base cases: j past the pattern → true; i past s with j remaining → false.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Because the pattern is matched greedily even in recursion (once a needed character is found, taking it is safe), the recursion depth is O(n) and each character is visited a constant number of times → O(n) time, O(n) stack space.
approaches.explanation:
Express the definition directly: `pat` is a subsequence of `s` starting at offsets `i, j` if either the pattern is exhausted (`j == len(pat)` → true), or `s` is exhausted first (false), or we match `s[i]` against `pat[j]` when equal and otherwise skip `s[i]`.

**Why it's correct.** It mirrors the formal recursive definition of 'subsequence', so it cannot be wrong.

**Why we don't ship it.** Recursion adds call-stack overhead and risks deep frames for long inputs, all to express something a single `for` loop captures cleanly. It's useful as a conceptual bridge — note that whenever `s[i] == pat[j]` you can *safely* consume the match (no need to also explore skipping it), which is exactly the greedy insight the iterative version exploits.
approaches.insight: The recursion has a special property: when characters match, you never need to explore *not* taking the match. That collapses the branching recursion into a deterministic single forward scan — the greedy two-pointer.

approaches.name: Greedy Two-Pointer Scan (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want — one pass, advance the pattern index only on matches.
hints: Keep an index j into 'hackerrank'. What do you do with j as you read each character of s?
If the current character equals pat[j], advance j; otherwise leave j alone and move on.
After scanning s, the answer is YES exactly when j reached the length of the pattern.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single sweep over s with O(1) work per character → O(n) time. Only two integer pointers are kept → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Hold a pointer `j` into the target word `"hackerrank"`. Scan `s` left to right; whenever the current character equals `pat[j]`, advance `j`. After the scan, return `"YES"` iff `j` reached the end of the pattern.

**Why greedy (earliest match) is optimal.** Suppose `pat[j]` first occurs at position `p` in the remaining input. Matching it at `p` rather than some later position `p' > p` can only help: it leaves the longer suffix `s[p+1:]` available for the rest of the pattern, which is a superset of `s[p'+1:]`. So if any valid matching exists, the greedy earliest-match matching also exists. There's never a reason to pass up the first opportunity.

**Why advance only on a match.** `j` represents 'how much of the pattern is already placed'. Bumping it without a real match would claim progress that didn't happen, accepting strings that aren't actually supersequences.

**Why the success test is `j == len(pat)`.** Reaching the end of `s` proves nothing; what matters is whether all ten pattern letters got placed. The double `r` falls out naturally — after the first `r` matches, `j` points at the second `r` and waits for another one.

**Why O(1) space.** Just two indices; no recursion, no auxiliary structures.
approaches.insight: Subsequence existence is the canonical greedy-pointer problem: a single forward sweep with a pattern cursor that only moves on a hit. The 'earliest match is safe' argument is the same exchange argument behind many greedy proofs.

pitfalls: Using contains/indexOf — that tests substring, not subsequence.
Advancing j on non-matches, accepting strings that aren't supersequences.
Returning based on i reaching the end of s instead of j reaching the pattern length.

commonMistakes: Treating it as a substring (contiguous) search instead of a subsequence.
Advancing the pattern pointer when characters don't match.
Checking the wrong termination condition (end of s rather than end of pattern).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Substring instead of subsequence
commonMistakesDetailed.why: 'hackerrank' rarely appears contiguously; the problem allows gaps. Using contains() returns NO for valid inputs like 'hhaacckk…'.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Advancing the pattern pointer on mismatch
commonMistakesDetailed.why: j tracks confirmed progress through the pattern. Bumping it without a match fabricates matches and accepts strings missing required letters.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong success condition
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The answer depends on whether the pattern was fully matched, not on consuming all of s. Test j == len(pattern).

patternNote: Greedy subsequence matching. To test whether a fixed pattern is a subsequence, keep a cursor into the pattern and advance it only on matches during a single pass. The earliest-match-is-safe exchange argument makes greedy optimal — the same idea powers Is Subsequence and Number of Matching Subsequences.
